name: Dom Luís I Bridge
short: The 1886 double-deck iron arch bridge designed by Théophile Seyrig, with the Metro on the upper deck and traffic and pedestrians below.
long: The Dom Luís I Bridge is Porto's most recognisable landmark and a symbol of the city. Its two-deck iron arch, with a 172-metre central span, links the Ribeira quay to Vila Nova de Gaia, and the upper deck offers one of the finest views over the Douro. Since 2005 the upper deck carries line D of the Porto Metro, while the lower deck serves public transport and pedestrians. The bridge forms part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing of Porto's historic centre.
history:
The idea of a new crossing over the Douro emerged in the 1870s, when the old suspension bridge, the Ponte Pênsil, could no longer cope with the growing city. In 1879 Gustave Eiffel proposed a single high-deck design, but it was rejected because Porto needed a more powerful two-deck crossing. In November 1880 a competition was launched, with entries from Eiffel as well as Belgian and British firms.

The project by the Belgian Société de Willebroek won, authored by Théophile Seyrig, a former partner of Eiffel and the designer of the Maria Pia Bridge. The first stone was laid on 21 November 1881, and the bridge was inaugurated on 31 October 1886; the lower deck was completed a year later.

The structure is a two-hinged wrought-iron arch system whose central arch has a span of 172 metres, the longest of its kind in the world when it was built. The upper deck rises about 60 metres above the water, while the lower deck links the Ribeira on the Porto side to Avenida Diogo Leite in Gaia.

In 1908 trams began using the upper deck, and on 27 June 2003 it was closed to cars and adapted for line D of the Porto Metro, opened on 18 September 2005. After repairs between 2021 and 2023, the lower deck was reserved for public transport, taxis, cyclists and pedestrians. In 1996 the bridge was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
facts: Inaugurated on 31 October 1886; the first stone was laid on 21 November 1881.
Its 172 m central arch was a record among metal bridges of its time.
The upper deck runs about 60 m above the Douro and carries Metro line D.
The design was by Théophile Seyrig, a former partner of Gustave Eiffel.
It replaced the Ponte Pênsil and is part of the UNESCO listing since 1996.
tip: Climb to the upper deck at sunset: the view over Ribeira, the Serra do Pilar monastery and the Douro valley is at its best. The upper deck is pedestrian and Metro-only, the lower deck is for public transport.
